# Cellulations and homology

Let a closed surface $\Sigma$ be decomposed into vertices, edges, and faces. Its cellular chain complex is

$$
C_2\xrightarrow{\partial_2}C_1\xrightarrow{\partial_1}C_0,
\qquad
\partial_1\partial_2=0.
$$

The first homology group is

$$
H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb F_2)
=\ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2.
$$

Cycles in $\operatorname{im}\partial_2$ bound collections of faces and are homologically trivial. Nontrivial homology classes are cycles that cannot be contracted through the cellulation.

::: {#def-hyperbolic-homological-css .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: homological CSS code

Place one physical qubit on every edge and define

$$
H_X=\partial_1,
\qquad
H_Z=\partial_2^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Rows of $H_X$ are vertex-star $X$ checks; rows of $H_Z$ are face-boundary $Z$ checks. Since

$$
H_XH_Z^{\mathsf T}=\partial_1\partial_2=0,
$$

all stabilizers commute.
:::

With this convention, $Z$-type logical operators are nontrivial primal homology classes and $X$-type logical operators are nontrivial dual homology classes. Exchanging $X$ and $Z$ gives an equivalent convention.

::: {#thm-hyperbolic-surface-parameters .callout-important icon="false"}
## (closed orientable surface code)

For a connected cellulation of a closed orientable surface of genus $g$, the homological CSS code has

$$
n=|E|,
\qquad
k=\dim H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb F_2)=2g.
$$

Its $Z$ distance is the length of the shortest nontrivial primal cycle, and its $X$ distance is the length of the shortest nontrivial dual cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof of the dimension formula

For a connected closed cellulation, $\operatorname{rank}\partial_1=|V|-1$. Because the sum of all face boundaries vanishes and this is the only dependency for a connected closed orientable surface, $\operatorname{rank}\partial_2=|F|-1$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
k
&=|E|-\operatorname{rank}\partial_1-\operatorname{rank}\partial_2\\
&=|E|-|V|-|F|+2\\
&=2-(|V|-|E|+|F|)\\
&=2-\chi(\Sigma)=2g.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

Surfaces with boundary require relative homology: different boundary types determine which chains may terminate and therefore which logical strings exist [@bombin2007homological].

# Regular tilings

A regular tiling of type $\{r,s\}$ has $r$ edges around every face and $s$ faces meeting at every vertex. If $n=|E|$, double counting gives

$$
|F|=\frac{2n}{r},
\qquad
|V|=\frac{2n}{s}.
$$

For a closed orientable quotient,

$$
\chi=|V|-|E|+|F|
=n\left(\frac2s-1+\frac2r\right).
$$

Therefore

$$
k=2-\chi
=2+n\left(1-\frac2r-\frac2s\right).
$$

::: {#def-hyperbolic-tiling-regime .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: geometric regime

A regular $\{r,s\}$ tiling is

$$
\begin{cases}
\text{spherical},&\frac1r+\frac1s>\frac12,\\
\text{Euclidean},&\frac1r+\frac1s=\frac12,\\
\text{hyperbolic},&\frac1r+\frac1s<\frac12.
\end{cases}
$$
:::

In the hyperbolic case, $1-2/r-2/s>0$, so suitable compact quotients have asymptotically nonzero rate. For standard families of two-dimensional hyperbolic surface codes, the systole—and hence distance—typically grows as $O(\log n)$ rather than $O(\sqrt n)$ [@breuckmann2016constructions].

# LDPC properties and tradeoffs

For a $\{r,s\}$ cellulation:

- each face $Z$ check has weight $r$;
- each vertex $X$ check has weight $s$; and
- every edge qubit participates in two checks of each type on a closed manifold.

Fixed $r$ and $s$ therefore give a quantum LDPC family. Increasing $r$ or $s$ can improve the asymptotic rate formula but also increases stabilizer weight. The hyperbolic metric supplies local adjacency intrinsically, yet embedding the quotient into a planar hardware layout generally requires nonlocal couplers or routing overhead.

The central comparison is

| Family | Asymptotic rate | Typical distance scaling | Native planar locality |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Euclidean toric/surface code | vanishing | $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ | yes |
| 2D hyperbolic surface code | constant | $O(\log n)$ | no in a flat embedding |

: Geometric tradeoff for common homological-code families.

Constant rate does not by itself imply superior logical performance at practical sizes. Check weights, finite systoles, syndrome-extraction circuits, and decoder behavior all matter.

# Decoding

Under independent $X$ or $Z$ noise with perfect syndrome measurement, each error chain has a boundary consisting of violated checks. A matching decoder pairs these defects along short paths, exactly as described in [Maximum-Likelihood Decoding and MWPM](../decoding/maximum-likelihood-and-mwpm.qmd). The correction fails when the union of actual and inferred chains contains a nontrivial homology class.

Matching algorithms developed for Euclidean surface codes can be applied to the finite decoding graph of a hyperbolic code, but their thresholds and finite-size behavior differ. Breuckmann and Terhal provide explicit compact constructions and numerical threshold estimates [@breuckmann2016constructions]. Other approaches exploit local cellular automata, union-find ideas, or message passing; no decoder should be described as geometry-independent without specifying its graph construction and noise assumptions.

# Logical operations

Nontrivial cycles support logical Pauli strings. More general fault-tolerant logical operations can be implemented through code deformation, lattice surgery, mapping-class-group actions, or code switching, depending on the available geometry. A high encoding rate complicates routing and selective access to individual logical qubits: algebraic existence of many homology classes does not automatically provide a low-depth local gate set.

The transversal-gate constraints discussed in [Triorthogonal Codes and Transversal $T$ Gates](triorthogonal-codes.qmd) are complementary. Homological geometry supplies locality and logical topology, whereas triorthogonality supplies a divisibility condition for a non-Clifford transversal operation.
